title: Kopo Kopo's Turn From Microlenders to Nairobi's Small Shops
dek: Between 2011 and 2012 Dylan Higgins and Ben Lyon dropped their first customers, became a for-profit company and bet on helping Kenyan merchants accept M-Pesa.

story.event: Turning a microfinance payments project into a service for Kenyan merchants to accept M-Pesa
story.summary: Kopo Kopo began in 2010 as a non-profit mobile microcredit project in Sierra Leone. In late 2011 its American co-founders Dylan Higgins and Ben Lyon became a for-profit company in Kenya, turned from microfinance institutions to merchants of every kind, and in March 2012 launched a service letting small businesses accept M-Pesa through Safaricom. It reached about 10,000 merchants by late 2013; in 2015 the company shifted to merchant cash advances and the founders handed over to a new chief executive.
paragraphs: In April 2012 the twelve staff of Kopo Kopo moved into a new office on the second floor of the Bishop Magua building in Nairobi. Its American co-founders, Dylan Higgins and Ben Lyon, had come by a winding road. The company began in 2010 as a non-profit project: Lyon, then in Freetown, wanted a mobile system for microcredit, and the name came from the Krio word for money. Higgins described a proof of concept built in a Seattle basement and a pilot running in Sierra Leone within six months. The founders later admitted they had been "way too early"; few people there used mobile money.

Kenya was the opposite. Seven in ten Kenyans used M-Pesa, yet by Kopo Kopo's own 2011 count fewer than 0.01 per cent of businesses had an M-Pesa merchant account; Higgins later recalled Safaricom having about 100. Microfinance institutions, their first customers, proved slow to adopt anything new. "I knew it, but it didn't click until I was out here," Higgins said of M-Pesa's reach. The founders made two changes: from non-profit to for-profit, with Kopo Kopo incorporated in Kenya in August 2011, and, once talks with Safaricom began late that year, from serving microlenders to serving any business.

Money was hard to find. Higgins said they had to leave Africa to raise it and spoke to more than 100 investors in the US and Europe, who called them "too early, too small". In October 2011 Khosla Impact and BlueOrchard invested. It took "many months", Higgins said, to get Safaricom comfortable with taking M-Pesa to the point of sale. The Kenyan service launched in March 2012: a shop got a short number its customers could pay much as they bought airtime. The first six months went on proving that thousands of merchants would want it.

They did. By late 2013 Kopo Kopo had about 10,000 merchants and a $2.6 million Series A, but Safaricom, having seen the market, was competing for the same shops. "We've had to have a philosophy that we are growing the whole pie," Higgins said. In 2015 the company shifted its focus to cash advances for merchants, and Higgins and Lyon handed over to a new chief executive, Ken Kinyua, staying on as shareholders.

quote.text: the account of particular cases is yet more lacking in exactness; for they do not fall under any art or precept but the agents themselves must in each case consider what is appropriate to the occasion, as happens also in the art of medicine or of navigation.
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle says no rulebook settles a particular case; the person acting has to judge what fits the occasion, as a doctor or a navigator does. Higgins knew M-Pesa's numbers from afar, but by his own account the opportunity only became clear once he was standing in Nairobi.

reflection: What changed at Kopo Kopo was the customer more than the purpose. The founders still wanted small businesses to handle money more safely; they stopped waiting for microlenders to want it and went where people were already paying by phone. Higgins told an interviewer in 2012 that the biggest mistake is "holding on to their original idea" until it becomes an ego-trip.

You may carry a picture, formed long ago, of who your work is for. It is worth checking now and then whether the people actually reaching for it are the ones you pictured, and being curious rather than disappointed if they are not.
invitation: Write down who you first imagined using the piece of work you are most attached to, and beside it who has actually asked for it this year. If the two differ, leave the page for a day before deciding anything.

cross_checks.claim: Kopo Kopo's original concept served microfinance institutions, and the founders changed to serving all merchants
The Kenyan merchant service launched in March 2012
Very few Kenyan businesses could accept M-Pesa when Kopo Kopo began
The idea began in a Seattle basement with a pilot in Sierra Leone
Khosla Impact was an early investor, and a $2.6 million Series A followed in late 2013
In 2015 Kopo Kopo shifted to merchant cash advances and the founders handed over to Ken Kinyua

research_notes: Merchant accounts before Kopo Kopo: Higgins told PandoDaily (2013) that Safaricom had 'just 100 formal merchant accounts'; Ben Lyon told Business Daily (2014) that Safaricom had signed only three firms (Woolworths, Deacons, Bata) on its buy-goods service; GSMA (2014) reports Kopo Kopo's 2011 calculation that fewer than 0.01% of Kenyan businesses had an M-Pesa merchant account; Business Daily also says 1% of businesses accepted e-payments. The story gives the GSMA figure and Higgins's 100, both attributed. Early funding: PandoDaily reports $130,000 from friends and family and a $725,000 seed round from Khosla Impact; VC4A (2012) says Khosla Impact and BlueOrchard invested in October 2011; PYMNTS (2013) refers to $1 million in previous venture funding. The story names the October 2011 investors and gives no seed amount. Series A: $2.6 million (PandoDaily, PYMNTS, HumanIPO) in November 2013. Merchant counts rise over time and are consistent: about 10,000 (PandoDaily, November 2013), 12,500 (GSMA, April 2014), 15,000+ (TechMoran, August 2014). Origin: VC4A and PYMNTS (2011) give the Sierra Leone microcredit and Seattle-basement origin; Business Daily (2014) says the three founders registered the company in the US in 2010 to serve small businesses but found the market saturated. The story follows the founders' own earlier accounts. Third co-founder Tom Bostlemann (PandoDaily, Business Daily) stayed in the US and is not named in the story. GSMA's product summary gives 'Year launched: 2011' but its text gives the Kenyan launch as March 2012, as does TechMoran; the story uses March 2012. The 'way too early' remark in VC4A is not clearly attributed to one founder, so the story says 'the founders'. The PandoDaily article is cited from a copy on a Pace University course page because the original page did not show the article text to the verifier. TechCabal's 2015 report is syndicated at NextBillion with the same text; it is used as one source. The Aristotle passage concerns ethics in general; it is applied by analogy.
